# 15 Halogen compounds

本章只覆盖 AS 3.3 Halogen Compounds：halogenoalkanes 的命名、反应和机制，C–X 键与水解速率，以及 CFCs 和 ozone depletion。下方题目来自 **3.3 Halogen Compounds** 原题；无法独立提取的题图没有截图加入。

## Learning objectives

- identify primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes;
- explain nucleophilic substitution and distinguish S<sub>N</sub>1/S<sub>N</sub>2;
- predict products with OH<sup>−</sup>, CN<sup>−</sup> and NH<sub>3</sub>;
- use silver nitrate to compare halogenoalkane hydrolysis;
- explain the stability and environmental impact of CFCs.

## 15.1 Halogenoalkanes and the C–X bond

A halogenoalkane has a halogen attached to an alkyl group, R–X. The carbon bonded to the halogen is δ<sup>+</sup> because halogen is more electronegative; it is attacked by nucleophiles. A **primary** halogenoalkane has the C–X carbon bonded to one other carbon, a secondary to two, and a tertiary to three.

The C–X bond strength decreases down the group: C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I. Thus iodoalkanes hydrolyse fastest and chloroalkanes slowest (among Cl, Br and I). In warm ethanol/water with aqueous AgNO<sub>3</sub>, released halide gives AgCl white, AgBr cream, or AgI yellow precipitate. The rate follows RI > RBr > RCl because less bond energy is needed to break C–I.

## 15.2 Nucleophilic substitution

Nucleophiles donate a lone pair to the δ<sup>+</sup> carbon and replace X<sup>−</sup>. Aqueous OH<sup>−</sup> gives an alcohol; ethanolic CN<sup>−</sup> gives a nitrile; excess ethanolic NH<sub>3</sub> under pressure gives an amine.

<div class="equation-block">R–Br + OH<sup>−</sup> → R–OH + Br<sup>−</sup><br>R–Br + CN<sup>−</sup> → R–CN + Br<sup>−</sup><br>R–Br + 2NH<sub>3</sub> → R–NH<sub>2</sub> + NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + Br<sup>−</sup></div>

Using CN<sup>−</sup> is valuable because it adds one carbon atom to the chain. Acid hydrolysis of the nitrile then gives a carboxylic acid.

Primary halogenoalkanes normally react by **S<sub>N</sub>2**: one concerted step, with nucleophile attack and C–X breaking simultaneously; the rate depends on both halogenoalkane and nucleophile. Tertiary halogenoalkanes usually react by **S<sub>N</sub>1**: slow heterolytic C–X fission makes a carbocation, then rapid nucleophile attack; the rate depends only on halogenoalkane concentration.

## 15.3 Elimination and preparation

Hot ethanolic OH<sup>−</sup> promotes elimination: H and X are removed from adjacent atoms to form C=C, for example CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + OH<sup>−</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + Br<sup>−</sup>. Aqueous OH<sup>−</sup> instead favours substitution. Halogenoalkanes are also formed by free-radical substitution of alkanes with Cl<sub>2</sub>/UV, and by electrophilic addition of HX or X<sub>2</sub> to alkenes.

## 15.4 CFCs and ozone depletion

CFCs were useful as refrigerants and propellants because they are inert, non-flammable and non-toxic at ground level. Strong C–F bonds help their stability. Their long lifetime lets them diffuse to the stratosphere, where UV radiation causes homolytic bond fission and releases chlorine radicals.

<div class="equation-block">CCl<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> → CClF<sub>2</sub>· + Cl·<br>Cl· + O<sub>3</sub> → ClO· + O<sub>2</sub><br>ClO· + O → Cl· + O<sub>2</sub></div>

Chlorine radical is regenerated, so one radical can catalyse the destruction of many ozone molecules. Ozone normally absorbs harmful UV radiation; CFC manufacture has therefore been phased out under the Montreal Protocol.

### Question 2 · 3.3 SQ Easy Q2(a-c)
<p>Propane is converted into 1-chloropropane (step 1), then propene (step 2).</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> State conditions and mechanism for step 1.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Write both propagation equations.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Name the mechanism in step 2 and state reagent and conditions.</p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>Cl<sub>2</sub>, UV light; free-radical substitution.</li><li>Cl· + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> → HCl + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>·; CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>· + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl + Cl·.</li><li>Elimination; hot ethanolic KOH/NaOH.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-03}
### Question 3 · 3.3 SQ Easy Q3(a-c)
![Fig. 3.1 Incomplete SN1 mechanism](../assets/questions/extracted/15/independent/sq-easy-q3-fig-3-1.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Incomplete two-step SN1 mechanism for 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with hydroxide ions" style="filter: invert(1);"}
<p><strong>(a)</strong> State what is meant by a tertiary halogenoalkane and what the numbers 1 and 2 refer to in S<sub>N</sub>1 and S<sub>N</sub>2.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Complete the S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism for 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with hydroxide ions and identify the rate-determining step.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Excess ethanolic ammonia is heated under pressure with 2-bromo-2-methylpropane: draw the product and state its functional group.</p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>The C bonded to X is attached to three carbon atoms; 1/2 indicate the number of species in the rate-determining step.</li><li>Slow C–Br heterolytic fission forms a tertiary carbocation and Br<sup>−</sup>; rapid OH<sup>−</sup> attack follows. Step 1 is rate determining.</li><li>(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CNH<sub>2</sub>, a primary amine.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-04}
### Question 4 · 3.3 SQ Medium Q1(a-e)
<p><strong>(a)</strong> State the H–C–H bond angle at terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> in propene.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> State fully the type of reaction when propene forms 1,2-dichloropropane.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> State conditions and type of reaction for ethane + chlorine → chloroethane + HCl.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Use bond enthalpy ideas to explain why iodine does not make iodoethane from ethane.</p>
<p><strong>(e)</strong> Complete possible radical equations in formation of chloroethane.</p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>120°.</li><li>Electrophilic addition.</li><li>UV light; free-radical substitution.</li><li>H abstraction by I· is energetically unfavourable, so the chain process is not sustained.</li><li>CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>· + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl + Cl·; valid termination equations combine radicals.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-05}
### Question 5 · 3.3 SQ Medium Q2(a-e)
![Fig. 2.1 Reaction scheme from 1-chloropropane](../assets/questions/extracted/15/independent/sq-medium-q2-fig-2-1.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Reaction scheme showing 1-chloropropane forming propene, butanenitrile and propan-1-amine"}
![Fig. 2.2 Concentration-time graph](../assets/questions/extracted/15/independent/sq-medium-q2-fig-2-2.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Concentration of a tertiary chloroalkane plotted against time"}
<p>1-chloropropane reacts to form propene, butanenitrile and propan-1-amine.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> State reagents/conditions for each, including the product with aqueous NaOH.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> A tertiary chloroalkane reacts with aqueous alkali: calculate rate from the given concentration graph.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Classify its mechanism.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Give AgNO<sub>3</sub>/ethanol observations and rate order for 1-chloro-, 1-bromo- and 1-iodobutane.</p>
<p><strong>(e)</strong> Draw the HBr addition mechanism to 2-methylpropene.</p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>Hot ethanolic OH<sup>−</sup> gives propene; KCN/ethanol under reflux gives butanenitrile; excess ethanolic NH<sub>3</sub> under pressure gives propan-1-amine; aqueous OH<sup>−</sup> under reflux gives propan-1-ol.</li><li>Use gradient of tangent at 50 s, with units mol dm<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>.</li><li>S<sub>N</sub>1.</li><li>AgBr is cream; RI &gt; RBr &gt; RCl.</li><li>Electrophilic addition via tertiary carbocation, then Br<sup>−</sup> attack.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-06}
### Question 6 · 3.3 SQ Hard Q1(a-d)
<p>A student compares rates of hydrolysis of six halogenoalkanes using ethanol, a 50 °C water bath and AgNO<sub>3</sub>.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> Suggest improvements to the method and state the reaction type other than precipitation.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Describe/explain two factors that affect rate.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Aqueous 1-bromopentane reacts with aqueous NaOH: identify the mechanism, number of steps, bromine-containing product and changed conditions that give three products.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> 1-chloropentane is prepared from an alcohol and SOCl<sub>2</sub>: give equation/state symbols and a justified safety precaution.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li><strong>(a)</strong> Control volumes/concentrations, use identical apparatus and a thermostated bath, repeat trials. The organic reaction is hydrolysis/nucleophilic substitution.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Rate increases with weaker C–X bond and with less steric hindrance / a more stable carbocation where S<sub>N</sub>1 applies.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> S<sub>N</sub>2, one step; NaBr; using ethanolic NaOH also permits elimination.</li><li><strong>(d)</strong> CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>OH(l) + SOCl<sub>2</sub>(l) → CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl(l) + SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + HCl(g). Use a fume cupboard because acidic/toxic gases are released.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-07}
### Question 7 · 3.3 SQ Hard Q2(a-d)
<p>2-bromo-2-methylpropane is refluxed with ethanolic KOH.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> Name products and mechanisms.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Explain the mixture of alkene and alcohol.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Give the equation between butan-2-ol and PI<sub>3</sub>.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Explain why sulfuric acid cannot be used to prepare an iodoalkane.</p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>2-methylpropene by elimination and 2-methylpropan-2-ol by nucleophilic substitution.</li><li>Ethanolic OH<sup>−</sup> favours elimination but water present can act as nucleophile, producing some alcohol.</li><li>3CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + PI<sub>3</sub> → 3CH<sub>3</sub>CH(I)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub>.</li><li>Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> oxidises I<sup>−</sup>/HI to I<sub>2</sub> rather than only generating HI.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-08}
### Question 8 · 3.3 SQ Hard Q3(a-c)
![Fig. 3.1 Reaction scheme for compounds G and H](../assets/questions/extracted/15/independent/sq-hard-q3-fig-3-1.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Reaction scheme showing compound G forming compound H and a nitrile" style="filter: invert(1);"}
<p>A chloroalkane G forms an alkene H and a nitrile. H does not show geometrical isomerism.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> Draw G and H.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> State reagents/conditions for reaction A.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Name and draw the mechanism for reaction B, including charges, lone pairs and curly arrows.</p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>H is an alkene in which one C of C=C has two identical groups; G is the matching chloroalkane.</li><li>Reaction A uses hot ethanolic OH<sup>−</sup> for elimination.</li><li>Reaction B is nucleophilic substitution with KCN in ethanol under reflux: the CN<sup>−</sup> lone pair attacks Cδ<sup>+</sup> and the C–Cl bond electrons move to Cl.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-09}
### Question 9 · 3.3 SQ Hard Q4(a-f)
![Apparatus for producing and collecting gaseous butenes](../assets/questions/extracted/15/independent/sq-hard-q4-apparatus.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Gas syringe and reflux condenser apparatus for producing gaseous butenes"}
<p>Bromobutanes react with hot ethanolic KOH to produce gaseous butenes.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> State purpose of the condenser.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Give a test for the functional group in the gas.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Calculate percentage conversion from given amount and gas volume.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Use gas volumes before/after cooling to calculate temperature.</p>
<p><strong>(e)</strong> Identify reaction/mechanism forming butan-1-ol and give an alcohol test.</p>
<p><strong>(f)</strong> Draw alkene isomers from 2-bromobutane.</p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>The condenser prevents loss of volatile ethanol/reactants while heating under reflux.</li><li>Bromine water decolourises, confirming C=C.</li><li>Use pV=nRT at the stated conditions, then compare moles of alkene with initial 0.0080 mol.</li><li>At constant pressure, V/T is constant.</li><li>Nucleophilic substitution by OH<sup>−</sup>; use acidified dichromate(VI), orange to green on warming, to confirm a primary alcohol.</li><li>But-1-ene, cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-10}
### Question 10 · 3.3 SQ Medium Q3(a-d)
![Fig. 3.1 Reaction scheme for 1-bromobutane](../assets/questions/extracted/15/independent/sq-medium-q3-fig-3-1.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Reaction scheme showing reactions of 1-bromobutane with aqueous and ethanolic sodium hydroxide"}
<p>1-bromobutane is prepared from KBr, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and butan-1-ol.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> Write the equations for HBr formation and the alcohol reaction.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> State two other preparations of 1-bromobutane.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Complete the reaction scheme from 1-bromobutane using aqueous/ethanolic NaOH and oxidation.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Explain why hydrolysis with aqueous AgNO<sub>3</sub> is slower than with aqueous NaOH.</p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>KBr + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → KHSO<sub>4</sub> + HBr; CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>OH + HBr → CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>Br + H<sub>2</sub>O.</li><li>For example butan-1-ol with PBr<sub>3</sub>, or substitution of a suitable butane derivative under stated conditions.</li><li>Aqueous OH<sup>−</sup> gives butan-1-ol then oxidation gives butanoic acid; ethanolic OH<sup>−</sup> gives but-1-ene, then hot acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves it.</li><li>AgNO<sub>3</sub> provides only water as the attacking nucleophile, whereas OH<sup>−</sup> is a stronger, negatively charged nucleophile.</li></ol></details>
:::
